paragraphs: Shared resources create a conflict between individual gain and collective sustainability. Taking more from a fishery or water supply may benefit one person while weakening the resource everyone relies on. The paper studies this tension in environments where resources change across both space and time, making behavior more complicated than a single decision about how much to take.

The authors model resource appropriation as a partially observed Markov game populated by independently learning agents. Each agent learns through deep reinforcement learning, allowing the researchers to examine behavior that emerges through repeated interaction. This provides a way to generate predictions for richer, real-time environments where the standard game-theoretic methods discussed in the abstract no longer apply.

The experiments highlight the importance of trial-and-error learning and explore connections among exclusion, sustainability, and inequality. Their contribution is a computational approach for studying how these outcomes develop together. The stated findings illuminate those relationships without establishing that independently learning agents invariably cooperate or invariably exhaust shared resources.
neurips-2017-a-multi-agent-reinforcement.tldr: Deep reinforcement learning models how independently learning agents share resources, revealing connections among learning, exclusion, sustainability, and inequality.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo generates samples by repeatedly moving between possible states. General-purpose movement rules can converge slowly, while specialized rules often require expert design. A-NICE-MC addresses this tradeoff by learning flexible transition rules, aiming to make the sampling process suit the distribution of interest automatically.

The method first uses adversarial training to teach a Markov chain to imitate a supplied data distribution without requiring likelihood evaluation for that training procedure. It then uses flexible, volume-preserving flows to construct parameterized MCMC kernels. These learned transformations provide expressive proposals within an MCMC framework, connecting neural-network flexibility with the guarantees associated with MCMC.

For sampling a prescribed posterior distribution, the authors introduce a bootstrap procedure that iteratively improves both the model and its samples. Better samples support better training, and improved transitions support subsequent sampling. The reported experiments show significant gains over competing methods, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. These are empirical comparisons supporting automated, distribution-specific proposal design, rather than a claim that the learned sampler always dominates every alternative.
neurips-2017-a-nice-mc-adversarial-train.tldr: A-NICE-MC learns distribution-specific MCMC proposals through adversarial training and iterative sample improvement, with strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms assign weights to input elements so a neural network can concentrate on relevant information. This paper develops a framework that also controls how that attention is organized. Instead of only distributing weight across individual elements, attention can become sparse or concentrate on whole segments and groups, making its focus easier to interpret.

The construction starts with a smoothed maximum operator whose gradient converts real-valued scores into probabilities. Softmax and a slight generalization of sparsemax fit within this formulation. Adding structured penalties changes the resulting attention pattern, providing a common mathematical route to several kinds of focus. The authors also derive efficient forward and backward computations so these mechanisms can be trained through backpropagation.

The framework is evaluated on textual entailment, machine translation, and sentence summarization as a replacement for existing attention mechanisms. The reported results improve interpretability without sacrificing performance. On entailment and summarization specifically, the proposed mechanisms outperform standard softmax and sparsemax attention. The contribution therefore combines a unifying formulation with practical evidence that more structured attention can remain effective.
neurips-2017-a-regularized-framework-for.tldr: A regularized attention framework produces sparse or grouped focus, improving interpretability while preserving performance in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Restarting accelerated gradient methods can improve convergence under conditions weaker than strong convexity. However, choosing an effective restart schedule can require an unknown constant describing the objective. This paper develops an adaptive approach that uses the magnitude of the proximal gradient to decide when to restart and when to stop.

The central construction combines adaptive regularization with conditional restarting. Its analysis covers the Hölderian error bound condition, a broader setting than quadratic growth. This matters because favorable convergence can depend on the objective's geometry even when strong convexity is unavailable. The method aims to exploit that geometry without requiring the previously needed restart constant.

The authors give two specific consequences. For coercive, semi-algebraic objectives, proximal gradient convergence is essentially faster than 1/t. For objectives combining the listed norm regularizers with a convex, smooth, piecewise-quadratic loss, the proposed algorithm is parameter-free and has faster linear convergence than proximal gradient. That second result is global, not merely near a solution, and requires no additional assumptions such as a restricted eigenvalue condition.
neurips-2017-adaptive-accelerated-gradie.tldr: An adaptive restart method uses proximal-gradient magnitude to obtain faster convergence under Hölderian error bounds, with global guarantees for specified objective classes.

paragraphs: Software telemetry helps companies understand device usage, but repeatedly collecting it creates a privacy problem. Locally differentially private methods can provide strong protection for a single collection round while losing protection rapidly across repeated rounds. Counter data, such as daily application usage, makes this issue especially relevant because the same kind of measurement is collected regularly.

The paper develops local differential privacy mechanisms specifically for repeated counter collection. Their formal privacy guarantees continue to apply over arbitrarily long execution periods. The design therefore treats repeated reporting as part of the problem itself, rather than relying on the privacy guarantee of an isolated report.

For estimating population means and histograms, the mechanisms achieve accuracy comparable to, or even the same as, existing single-round methods. The authors evaluate them on real counter datasets to check the theoretical findings and report deployment by Microsoft across millions of devices. Together, these results indicate that continuing telemetry collection can retain useful aggregate accuracy while supporting the stated long-term privacy guarantees.
neurips-2017-collecting-telemetry-data-p.tldr: New local differential privacy mechanisms support repeated counter telemetry with long-term privacy guarantees and accuracy comparable to single-round methods.

paragraphs: Translation decoding must choose words before the complete sentence is available. Beam search reduces the number of candidate translations considered, but its one-step lookahead can favor choices that do not lead to the best final sentence. This paper adds a learned estimate of longer-term translation quality to help guide those choices.

The proposed value network receives the source sentence, the translation prefix already generated, and a candidate next word. It predicts the value of the resulting partial translation if the translation model completes it, with BLEU given as an example of the target quality measure. The authors use a recurrent network and train it from bilingual data.

At decoding time, candidate words are assessed using both their conditional probabilities from the translation model and their predicted long-term values. This supplements immediate plausibility with an estimate of eventual sentence quality. Experiments report significant translation-accuracy improvements across several translation tasks, supporting the usefulness of learned lookahead without claiming that it guarantees the globally best translation.
neurips-2017-decoding-with-value-network.tldr: A recurrent value network improves translation beam search by estimating how candidate words affect the quality of completed sentences.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a model for sequences of count vectors: observations that contain multiple counts at successive time steps. Its goal is to represent both the hidden structure within these observations and their dependence over time. The starting point is Poisson factor analysis, extended with neural networks and a deep latent structure.

The neural networks represent implicit distributions that capture relationships between time steps. Local implicit distributions describe complicated local relationships, while the deeper latent structure is used to capture longer-term dependence. This division gives the model a way to account for temporal behavior at more than one scale within a single probabilistic formulation.

Learning combines variational inference for the latent variables with gradient descent on losses derived from the variational distribution. The authors evaluate the model using synthetic and real-world datasets and report good fitting and prediction performance, together with interpretable latent structure. The stated contribution is therefore both predictive and representational: the model aims to describe how count sequences evolve while exposing hidden factors that help explain their organization.
neurips-2017-deep-dynamic-poisson-factor.tldr: A deep Poisson factorization model combines neural temporal dependencies with latent structure to fit and predict sequential count data.

paragraphs: The paper represents an object or object part using a capsule, a group of neurons with a vector-valued activity. The vector's length expresses the probability that the entity exists, while its direction expresses the entity's instantiation parameters. This lets a representation convey both presence and information about how an entity appears.

Lower-level capsules use transformation matrices to predict the parameters of higher-level capsules. A higher-level capsule becomes active when multiple predictions agree. The proposed iterative routing mechanism directs a lower-level capsule's output preferentially toward higher-level capsules whose activity vectors align strongly with its prediction, measured through their scalar product.

This agreement-based communication connects the representations at different levels: supporting evidence depends on whether their predictions fit together. The authors train a multilayer capsule system discriminatively and report state-of-the-art performance on MNIST. They also find it considerably better than a convolutional network at recognizing highly overlapping digits. Those results support the proposed representation and routing mechanism in the evaluated digit-recognition settings.
neurips-2017-dynamic-routing-between-cap.tldr: Capsules represent entity presence and parameters as vectors, using agreement-based routing to achieve strong digit-recognition results.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships becomes harder when unobserved variables can influence multiple observed variables. This paper studies how to choose interventions to recover both the relationships among observables and the existence and location of latent variables that could confound them. Its main concern is how many interventions that recovery requires.

The approach separates discovery into stages. It first learns the graph induced among observed variables, then uses that graph to find latent variables. For the first stage, a randomized algorithm uses O(d log² n) interventions, where d is graph degree. A deterministic alternative uses O(log n + l), where l is the longest directed path.

The latent-discovery algorithm uses O(d² log n) interventions and handles latent variables between both adjacent and nonadjacent observed variables. Combining it with the randomized first stage gives O(d log² n + d² log n) interventions, compared with O(n²) for the stated naive baseline. The bounds show how graph structure, especially degree, shapes the intervention requirement rather than making it depend only on the number of variables.
neurips-2017-experimental-design-for-lea.tldr: A staged intervention strategy learns observable causal structure and locates latent confounders with intervention bounds depending on graph structure.

paragraphs: Submodular objectives express a form of diminishing returns and arise in learning tasks involving utility, sensing, and network inference. Their continuous versions need not have the convexity properties that usually make optimization straightforward. This paper shows that projected gradient methods can nevertheless provide meaningful approximation guarantees for a specified class under convex constraints.

For monotone continuous DR-submodular functions, every fixed point of projected gradient ascent achieves at least half the global optimum. With stochastic gradients, the methods reach an expected objective value above OPT/2 minus ε after O(1/ε²) iterations. These guarantees establish useful solution quality even when the method does not find a global maximizer.

The analysis also addresses objectives defined as expectations over an unknown distribution of submodular functions, a setting naturally suited to stochastic gradients. Through continuous relaxations, the results connect to approximate optimization of discrete monotone submodular problems. Experiments on real data report the best utility among the compared continuous baselines while remaining computationally competitive. The theoretical claims retain their monotonicity and diminishing-returns conditions.
neurips-2017-gradient-methods-for-submod.tldr: Projected gradient methods obtain half-optimum approximation guarantees for monotone continuous DR-submodular maximization under convex constraints.

paragraphs: Additive regression models simplify high-dimensional prediction by combining separate contributions from predictor variables. Their weakness is that they can miss interactions: the relationship between a response and one predictor may depend on another predictor. This paper revisits group additive modeling, which allows predictors to contribute jointly within groups.

The authors formally define the intrinsic group additive structure relating predictors to the response. They then develop a kernel method that identifies this structure while estimating the associated nonparametric functions. A newly derived measure of structural complexity supplies the penalty, so choosing the grouping and fitting its predictive functions become parts of the same estimation procedure.

The paper establishes consistency for identifying the intrinsic grouping structure and evaluates the method in simulations and real-data applications. These results support its use for high-dimensional nonparametric regression when interactions need to be represented. The central contribution is to make the grouping itself a target of learning, rather than treating all predictor effects as separate or assuming the relevant interaction groups are already known.
neurips-2017-group-additive-structure-id.tldr: A complexity-penalized kernel method jointly learns interacting predictor groups and their regression functions, with a structure-identification consistency result.

paragraphs: Imitation learning aims to reproduce expert behavior without an explicit reward signal. Human demonstrations often contain substantial variation, however, and some of it reflects hidden factors that are not labeled or directly modeled. InfoGAIL addresses this variation by learning latent structure alongside the behavior being imitated.

The algorithm builds on Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning and infers that structure without supervision. Its aim is to produce both effective imitation and interpretable representations of complex behavioral data, including visual demonstrations. Representing hidden variation gives the model a way to distinguish different patterns within expert behavior instead of treating the demonstrations as one undifferentiated collection.

In driving experiments, a model trained on human demonstrations accurately reproduces a variety of behaviors and anticipates human actions from raw visual inputs. Compared with the evaluated baselines, it better captures the demonstrations' latent structure, often recovering factors with meaningful interpretations. The qualifier matters: the reported results support interpretable variation in these experiments without claiming that every learned latent factor necessarily has a clear semantic meaning.
neurips-2017-infogail-interpretable-imit.tldr: InfoGAIL learns hidden variation in expert demonstrations, enabling diverse imitation and often interpretable behavioral representations from visual inputs.

paragraphs: Neural image classifiers can change their predictions after carefully chosen changes to an input that are barely perceptible. Such adversarial perturbations raise a quantitative question: how much must the input change before a classification change becomes possible? This paper approaches that question through mathematical lower bounds on the required perturbation magnitude.

A lower bound identifies a threshold below which a perturbation cannot be large enough to change the classification covered by the bound. It does not, by itself, say that every larger change will cause an error or that a successful perturbation exists exactly at the threshold. This distinction makes the result a statement about guaranteed minimum size rather than a recipe for constructing attacks.

The authors derive these bounds for neural networks and experimentally verify them on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The work contributes to a formal characterization of adversarial behavior, an area where the abstract describes a proven explanation as still elusive. Its stated advance is therefore a mathematical constraint on vulnerability supported by experiments, rather than a complete explanation or elimination of adversarial examples.
neurips-2017-lower-bounds-on-the-robustn.tldr: The paper derives and experimentally verifies lower bounds on the perturbation magnitude needed to change a neural network's classification.

paragraphs: Combining information from different sources is difficult when their probability distributions differ. A Wasserstein barycenter summarizes several distributions while respecting their geometry through optimal transport. The paper addresses the computational cost of finding this summary, particularly when data arrive continuously or are processed across multiple sources.

The proposed algorithm is parallel, communication-efficient, and designed for streaming data. It accepts continuous input distributions directly and discretizes only the barycenter estimate, making the formulation semi-discrete. This avoids requiring discrete representations of every input distribution. It can also track nonstationary inputs, updating the estimated summary as the source distributions change over time.

The authors provide bounds on approximation quality as the barycenter discretization becomes finer, linking computational representation to the quality of the resulting summary. They demonstrate practical effectiveness by tracking moving distributions on a sphere and in a large-scale Bayesian inference task. Together, these contributions make geometry-aware distribution aggregation more practical while explicitly retaining an approximation in the barycenter representation.
neurips-2017-parallel-streaming-wasserst.tldr: A parallel streaming algorithm estimates Wasserstein barycenters from continuous distributions and tracks changing inputs while discretizing only the barycenter.

paragraphs: Causal discovery can draw on both observations of a system and data collected after interventions. The paper develops algorithms that use these two sources together to learn directed acyclic graphs. Its motivating setting is biological network discovery, where large-scale single-cell measurements create a need for efficient and reliable causal analysis.

The authors introduce two interventional adaptations of the Greedy SP algorithm. Both receive consistency guarantees under the faithfulness assumption, making that assumption central to the theoretical claim. Consistency concerns recovery with increasing data; it should not be read as a promise of exact recovery from every finite dataset. The algorithms are also nonparametric and can therefore be used with non-Gaussian data.

Performance is analyzed on simulated data, protein signaling measurements, and single-cell gene expression data. These evaluations connect the algorithmic proposal to the biological settings that motivate it. The main stated contribution is the combination of observational and interventional evidence with conditional consistency guarantees, extending permutation-based causal inference to settings where actively changing a system supplies additional information.
neurips-2017-permutation-based-causal-in.tldr: Two nonparametric causal-discovery algorithms combine observational and interventional data, with consistency guarantees under faithfulness.

paragraphs: Many deep-learning tasks need a training objective that measures how different two distributions are using only samples. Maximum mean discrepancy is one option, but the paper identifies sensitivity to kernel bandwidth, weak gradients, and large minibatch requirements as difficulties when using it for training. Population matching discrepancy offers an alternative based on matching sampled populations.

PMD is defined through the minimum-weight matching between samples from the two distributions. The authors prove that it is a strongly consistent estimator of the first Wasserstein metric. This connects a finite sample-matching calculation to a population-level distribution distance. They also provide an algorithm for learning distribution parameters with PMD as the objective.

The method is applied to domain adaptation and generative modeling. In the reported experiments, PMD addresses the identified MMD drawbacks and outperforms MMD in both task performance and convergence speed. The statistical result explains what distance the estimator approaches, while the experiments support its usefulness as a training signal in the two evaluated applications.
neurips-2017-population-matching-discrep.tldr: Population matching discrepancy estimates Wasserstein distance through sample matching and improves on MMD in the reported learning experiments.

paragraphs: Predictive State Recurrent Neural Networks combine ideas from recurrent neural networks and predictive state representations to filter observations and predict dynamical systems. The paper seeks to connect flexible recurrent computation with the structure of probabilistic state updates, bringing insights from both modeling traditions into one architecture.

PSRNNs combine information using bilinear transfer functions, which can be composed deeply. The authors show that these operations arise naturally in Bayes-filter state updates: observations can act as gates on belief states. Training combines backpropagation through time with initialization from two-stage regression, a statistically consistent learning algorithm for predictive state representations. This links the starting parameters to a structured statistical procedure before recurrent training.

The model can also be factorized using tensor decomposition, reducing its size and suggesting connections to multiplicative architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs. Across four datasets, the authors report better performance than several popular alternatives for dynamical-system modeling. These findings support the proposed combination of architecture, initialization, and training in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2017-predictive-state-recurrent-.tldr: PSRNNs connect recurrent neural computation with predictive-state filtering, combining statistical initialization, recurrent training, and compact tensor factorization.

paragraphs: Asking a useful question involves choosing what information to seek and how to express the request. This paper models that choice by representing questions as executable programs. A program takes the state of the world as input and returns an answer, giving questions a formal structure that can be combined and evaluated.

The model assigns probabilities across a compositional space of programs. It favors questions that are concise and informative in the current context. This connects the construction of a question with its learning value: the model considers both what the answer could reveal and the complexity of the program needed to ask for it.

The authors evaluate the approach against open-ended questions people ask while trying to understand an ambiguous game situation. The model predicts human question choices and generates novel questions absent from its training set. Comparisons among model variants indicate that both informativeness and complexity matter for human-like behavior. The results support a program-based account of question generation in the studied setting.
neurips-2017-question-asking-as-program-.tldr: A cognitive model generates human-like questions as programs, balancing how much they reveal against their complexity.

paragraphs: Reconstruct & Crush Network learns to distinguish two data distributions by assigning them opposing energy values. Training lowers the energy of positive samples and raises it for samples from another distribution, which may be negative or unlabeled. The adversarial relationship is therefore between how the model treats the two supplied populations.

In the autoencoder implementation, reconstruction error supplies the energy. The network learns to reproduce samples from the first distribution while reconstructing those from the second poorly. That error then serves as a general distance measure for unfamiliar data. The approach can address positive-and-unlabeled learning and covariate shift, including settings with imbalanced data.

The authors demonstrate the method across several data types and tasks: CIFAR images in a not-in-training setting, Amazon review text for positive-and-unlabeled learning, and Facebook bAbI dialogues for response classification and completion. The reported experiments support the approach's flexibility across these settings. Its unifying contribution is to use the same reconstruct-versus-crush training principle across different forms of data.
neurips-2017-reconstruct-crush-network-2.tldr: An energy-based autoencoder learns to reconstruct positive samples and poorly reconstruct another population, supporting several learning settings and data types.

paragraphs: Fairness has multiple definitions that can impose different requirements on a predictive model. This paper pursues a unified framework for accommodating such definitions and their combinations. It brings together privileged learning and distribution matching, treating fairness as something that can influence training and be evaluated alongside predictive error.

Protected attributes such as race and gender are used as privileged information during training but are unavailable at prediction time. The authors describe this as accelerating training and providing fairness through unawareness. They additionally express demographic parity, equalized odds, and equality of opportunity as comparisons between conditional distributions, using Hilbert-space distance measures to handle those comparisons within a common formulation.

Several existing models emerge as special cases of the framework. The paper also advocates presenting a Pareto frontier of error and unfairness, exposing alternative operating points rather than choosing a single tradeoff implicitly. Decision-makers can then select and take responsibility for a particular balance. The broad ambition is adaptable fairness modeling; the concrete formulation covers the named criteria and their distribution-matching representation.
neurips-2017-recycling-privileged-learni.tldr: A fairness framework combines protected information during training with distribution matching and exposes tradeoffs between predictive error and unfairness.

paragraphs: Decision support requires estimating what would happen if a particular action were taken. A model trained to predict observed outcomes may instead learn relationships tied to how actions were chosen in its training data. The paper shows that this sensitivity to the existing action policy can make conventional supervised prediction unreliable for guiding decisions.

The authors propose changing the learning objective to predict counterfactual outcomes. This targets the consequences of alternative actions rather than outcomes under the policy that generated the data. For decisions unfolding over time, they introduce the Counterfactual Gaussian Process, which predicts continuous-time trajectories under sequences of future actions.

The model is demonstrated on risk prediction and individualized treatment planning through what-if reasoning. In these tasks, the relevant output is a possible future progression associated with a proposed action sequence. The stated benefits support aligning prediction with the decision being considered. The central contribution is this shift in target, together with a temporal model designed to represent action-dependent future trajectories.
neurips-2017-reliable-decision-support-u.tldr: Counterfactual Gaussian Processes predict future trajectories under alternative action sequences to improve decision support beyond policy-dependent outcome prediction.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hypothesis test for whether a data-generating function belongs to a specified reproducing kernel Hilbert space whose structure is only partly known. This offers a way to test properties of an unknown relationship while allowing considerable flexibility in the functions used to describe it.

Using reproducing-kernel theory, the authors reduce the original question to a one-sided score test involving a single scalar parameter. They develop robustness to kernel misspecification and introduce an ensemble estimator for the null model to support test performance in small samples. The construction makes the quality of null-model estimation an explicit part of the testing procedure.

The method is applied to detecting nonlinear interactions between groups of continuous features. Evaluations vary both the data-generating function and the way the null model is estimated. The results connect underfitting and overfitting with false-positive behavior and statistical power, and reveal unexpected inferential consequences of common estimation choices, including maximum-likelihood kernel tuning. This shows why fitting a model and using it for a hypothesis test require closely coordinated choices.
neurips-2017-robust-hypothesis-test-for-.tldr: A kernel-based hypothesis test detects nonlinear effects while addressing kernel misspecification and the influence of null-model estimation on inference.

paragraphs: Generalized linear bandits make repeated choices while learning about their rewards. Existing methods can become expensive as either the number of rounds or the number of available arms increases. This paper addresses both scaling problems: maintaining the learning computation over time and searching a large set of candidate actions.

The GLOC construction converts an online learning algorithm into a generalized linear bandit algorithm using confidence sets. Applied to online Newton steps, it produces a low-regret method whose per-step time and space costs remain constant with respect to elapsed rounds. This avoids the at-least-linear growth in time described for earlier methods.

For large arm sets, the authors formulate action selection as inner-product search, enabling hashing and time sublinear in the number of arms. A new hash-compatible algorithm improves the dimensional dependence of the stated regret bound from d^(3/2) for a Thompson-sampling extension to d^(5/4), compared with d for GLOC. They also propose more accurate approximate hash-key computation. Preliminary experiments support the methods' benefits.
neurips-2017-scalable-generalized-linear.tldr: Online confidence-set construction and hashing make generalized linear bandits more scalable across both repeated rounds and large action sets.

paragraphs: Restarting an accelerated optimization method can further improve its convergence, but the benefit depends on the geometry of the objective near its minimum. This paper studies that connection through Hölderian error bounds. The Łojasiewicz inequality provides the motivation: such bounds hold almost generically for the convex optimization problems considered.

The authors clarify how these error bounds control the performance of restart schemes. Their constants quantify the relevant geometry, yet those constants are unobservable. Consequently, a theoretically optimal restart rule cannot simply be selected by reading off all the required quantities from the problem. The practical question is whether searching for a good rule loses the acceleration benefit.

The paper shows that optimal restart strategies are robust and that searching for the best scheme adds only a logarithmic factor to complexity relative to the optimal bound. This makes adaptation to unknown constants comparatively inexpensive in the analysis. The resulting claim is that restart schemes generically accelerate accelerated methods, preserving the abstract's qualified scope rather than promising an improvement for every convex objective.
neurips-2017-sharpness-restart-and-accel.tldr: Restart schemes exploit Hölderian error bounds to improve accelerated optimization, with only logarithmic overhead for searching an effective schedule.

paragraphs: A vision model can be uncertain because its observations are noisy or because the model itself lacks enough knowledge. The paper distinguishes these as aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The latter can be reduced with sufficient data, while the former concerns noise inherent in what is observed. The authors study the benefits of representing both.

Their Bayesian deep-learning framework combines epistemic uncertainty with input-dependent aleatoric uncertainty. Allowing observation noise to depend on the input means the model can represent different noise levels across observations. The framework is studied on per-pixel semantic segmentation and depth regression, connecting uncertainty modeling to predictions about image content and scene depth.

The explicit treatment of uncertainty also yields new training losses interpreted as learned attenuation. These losses make training more robust to noisy data, so uncertainty affects the learning process as well as how predictions are described. The authors report new state-of-the-art results on segmentation and depth-regression benchmarks. The findings support combining the two uncertainty types within the evaluated vision models.
neurips-2017-what-uncertainties-do-we-ne.tldr: A Bayesian vision framework models observation noise and model uncertainty together, producing noise-robust losses and strong segmentation and depth results.
